title: The Rainy Ticket
question: You paid $60 for an outdoor concert ticket. On the day, it pours rain and you feel a cold coming on. The money is nonrefundable. What is the rational choice?
choices: Go and suffer, so the $60 is not wasted
Go for exactly 60 minutes to earn the money back
Stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone
Sell the ticket at a loss to punish yourself
correctAnswer: Stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone
correctExplanation: Right. The $60 is gone whether you go or not — only tonight's comfort versus misery is still decided. Rational choice compares futures, not pasts.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stay home and rest, treating the $60 as already gone. Going 'so it isn't wasted' spends a miserable evening trying to rescue money that is unrescuable. Compare the two futures: cozy rest versus cold rain.
lessonContent:
Money already spent is gone from every future you can still choose.
Compare only what differs between your options going forward.
'Not wasting it' usually means wasting an evening on top.
Notice the tug: honoring past payments feels loyal but decides nothing.
Share this: name one ticket or booking you should skip this month.

title: The Dull Movie
question: Twenty minutes into a two-hour film, you are bored and checking your watch. Leaving now frees your whole evening. What should decide it?
choices: How you will spend the next hundred minutes
The price of the ticket you already paid
How annoyed the row behind you looks
The director's reputation from past films
correctAnswer: How you will spend the next hundred minutes
correctExplanation: Exactly. Only the remaining hundred minutes are still yours. The ticket, the reviews, and the director's past cannot be changed by staying.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is how you will spend the next hundred minutes. The ticket is sunk, the row's feelings are not yours to manage, and reputations don't refund evenings. Ask only: is this film the best use of the time I still hold?
lessonContent:
Time already spent is sunk exactly like money.
Ask what the next hour earns you, not what the last one cost.
Quitting fast is a skill, not a character flaw.
Boredom twenty minutes in reliably predicts the rest.
Share this: walk out of something dull this week — practice quitting.

title: The Heavy Book
question: You are 100 pages into a 400-page novel you dislike. Finishing takes six more hours you could spend on books you love. What is the smart move?
choices: Finish it, because 100 pages must not go to waste
Skim the ending so the 100 pages count double
Reread the 100 pages until you like them
Abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy
correctAnswer: Abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy
correctExplanation: Yes. The 100 pages bought information — this book isn't for you — and that information says stop. Six good hours beat six dutiful ones.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to abandon it and read something you will actually enjoy. The 100 pages already paid for their lesson by revealing the book's quality. Reading on converts a small sunk cost into a large one.
lessonContent:
A bad book's opening chapters are a paid sample, not a contract.
'Life's too short' is a decision rule, not a cliché.
Abandoning fast multiplies lifetime good books.
Track joy per hour and quit below your bar.
Share this: shelve one book you are enduring, today.

title: The Failing Project
question: Your team spent four months on a product that tests badly with every user group. Pivoting now saves the next six months. What argues for pivoting?
choices: The four months already invested in the current design
What the next six months will produce under each plan
The launch date printed on old slides
How hard everyone worked last quarter
correctAnswer: What the next six months will produce under each plan
correctExplanation: Correct. The four months are identical in every future — only the next six differ. Effort and old slides don't convert into user love.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is what the next six months will produce under each plan. Past effort is sunk; honoring it with more doomed effort doubles the loss. Kill criteria written in advance make pivots painless.
lessonContent:
Projects need kill criteria before attachment grows.
Past quarters never appear in any future you can pick.
Pivoting is redirecting, not failing.
Bad test results are cheap information — use them early.
Share this: write a kill rule for one project you own.

title: The Cold Meal
question: You ordered an expensive dish that arrives overcooked and unpleasant. Eating it will only spoil your evening further. What is rational?
choices: Stop eating and order something you will enjoy
Eat it all, since it cost so much
Eat half to recover half the value
Complain loudly until dessert is free
correctAnswer: Stop eating and order something you will enjoy
correctExplanation: Right. The bill is fixed; only your evening's pleasure is still variable. Forcing down bad food adds a ruined night to a wasted dish.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to stop eating and order something you will enjoy. The price cannot be uneaten, and half-measures recover no value at all. Fix the future (your evening), not the past (the bill).
lessonContent:
Fixed bills and variable evenings belong in separate columns.
Forcing consumption never refunds anything.
Half-measures split the difference between two bad options.
Speak up early: kitchens fix mistakes cheaper than stomachs do.
Share this: send back one bad dish instead of enduring it.

title: The Long Queue
question: You waited 30 minutes in a slow line, then spot an empty till across the store. Switching means losing your spot but checking out in two minutes. What matters?
choices: The 30 minutes you already waited
How annoyed the people behind you look
The principle of never switching lines
The minutes each option still requires
correctAnswer: The minutes each option still requires
correctExplanation: Exactly. The 30 minutes are spent in all futures; only remaining wait differs. Switching 'wastes' nothing — it buys back your time.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the minutes each option still requires. Loyalty to a line is loyalty to sunk minutes. Compare forward waits only, and the empty till wins by a mile.
lessonContent:
Queues charge in forward minutes, not past ones.
Line loyalty is sunk-cost loyalty with a trolley.
Switching lines feels disloyal and is usually brilliant.
Recompute waits whenever new information arrives.
Share this: switch one queue this week and time the savings.

title: The Sinking Stock
question: You bought shares at $100; they now trade at $40 and the company's prospects worsened. Fresh analysis says similar money earns more elsewhere. What should you do?
choices: Hold until $100 to avoid admitting the loss
Buy more to lower the average at any cost
Sell and move the money where prospects are better
Never look at the price again
correctAnswer: Sell and move the money where prospects are better
correctExplanation: Correct. The $60 loss is realized in every future; only the $40's future growth is still choosable. 'Getting back to even' is nostalgia priced in dollars.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to sell and move the money where prospects are better. The purchase price is history; each dollar should work where it grows best. Averaging down on worsening prospects throws good money after bad.
lessonContent:
Every dollar should work where it grows best, regardless of its history.
'Back to even' is an emotional target, not a strategy.
Losses are tuition only if they change future behavior.
Re-underwrite every holding as if you bought it today.
Share this: ask of one holding — would I buy it fresh today?

title: The Costly Auction
question: Bidding passes what the antique is worth to you, but you have already bid five times and hate losing. What is the disciplined move?
choices: Keep bidding to defend your earlier bids
Stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying
Bid once more to scare the rival off
Ask the auctioneer to cancel your bids
correctAnswer: Stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying
correctExplanation: Yes. Past bids are sunk; overpaying now converts a lost auction into an expensive trophy. Set your max before bidding and let rivals overpay.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to stop bidding, since earlier bids cannot be recovered by overpaying. Hating to lose is exactly the lever auctions pull. Your max price decided calmly beats your pride decided publicly.
lessonContent:
Set your walk-away price before the adrenaline starts.
Auctions monetize the hatred of losing — budget for it.
Each bid should stand alone, not defend its predecessors.
Winning an overpayment is just losing with applause.
Share this: set a max price before your next bid of any kind.

title: The Membership Trap
question: You prepaid a year of gym visits, then moved across town. Each trip now costs an hour you resent. What is the clear-eyed view?
choices: Treat the fee as gone and exercise near home
Go three times weekly to honor the payment
Drive across town angrily every single week
Cancel fitness entirely out of spite
correctAnswer: Treat the fee as gone and exercise near home
correctExplanation: Right. The fee is identical in all futures; weekly resentment is optional. Honoring payments with suffering is the sunk-cost signature.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to treat the fee as gone and exercise near home. Forced cross-town trips convert one sunk fee into fifty resented hours. Pay for the future you will actually use.
lessonContent:
Prepayments buy options, not obligations.
Resented compliance costs more than the fee ever did.
Re-optimize whenever your address, schedule, or body changes.
The best gym is the one your future self attends.
Share this: cancel one membership your routine outgrew.

title: The Overfull Plate
question: At a buffet you already paid for, you feel full but keep eating 'to get your money's worth.' What is this logic doing?
choices: Recovering money through extra bites
Beating the restaurant at its own game
Training your stomach for future buffets
Trading comfort and health for money already gone
correctAnswer: Trading comfort and health for money already gone
correctExplanation: Correct. The entry fee is sunk; extra bites purchase only discomfort. 'Money's worth' at a buffet is measured in enjoyment, which peaks before fullness.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is trading comfort and health for money already gone. No bite refunds the entry fee. Restaurants price buffets knowing full stomachs stop — the house banks on exactly this fallacy.
lessonContent:
'Getting your money's worth' peaks before discomfort begins.
Buffets are priced against this exact fallacy.
Fullness is a stop signal, not a challenge.
Worth is enjoyment per bite, and late bites score negative.
Share this: leave food on one buffet plate deliberately.

title: The Awful Layover
question: You booked a $200 flight with miserable layovers. Later a direct flight for the same trip appears at $180. The $200 is nonrefundable either way. What is rational?
choices: Endure the layovers so the $200 counts for something
Book the direct flight and let the $200 go
Buy the direct flight and also take the miserable one
Skip the trip to avoid deciding
correctAnswer: Book the direct flight and let the $200 go
correctExplanation: Yes. The $200 is gone in all futures; the choice is between comfort and misery at $180. Enduring layovers 'for the money' spends hours to honor a sunk fare.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to book the direct flight and let the $200 go. The old fare cannot be flown into value. Compare total futures: $200 lost plus comfort versus $200 lost plus exhaustion.
lessonContent:
Nonrefundable means the money is gone, not that the trip is fixed.
Rebook whenever a better option beats the old total.
'Getting use' from a bad booking spends good hours after bad dollars.
Separate the purchase (past) from the journey (future).
Share this: reprice one booking you assumed was final.

title: The Half Rewrite
question: Your team rewrote half the app before discovering a maintained library that does it better. Continuing wastes three months; switching wastes the rewrite. What is best?
choices: Finish the rewrite to justify the months spent
Rewrite the other half twice as fast out of pride
Adopt the library and scrap the rewrite
Hide the library so nobody feels embarrassed
correctAnswer: Adopt the library and scrap the rewrite
correctExplanation: Correct. The rewrite months are sunk; the next three are still yours. Scrapping feels wasteful but saves a quarter — pride is the most expensive dependency.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to adopt the library and scrap the rewrite. Sunk engineering effort is not architecture. The discovery is good news arriving late, not an insult — celebrate finding the shortcut in month two instead of month five.
lessonContent:
'We built it ourselves' is not a technical argument.
Discoveries that obsolete your work are gifts with awkward timing.
Prototype to learn, then be willing to throw the prototype away.
Measure remaining cost, never invested cost.
Share this: name one homegrown tool a library could replace.

title: The Silent Campaign
question: Half the ad budget is spent with zero qualified leads, and the data shows the channel mismatches your buyers. What should happen to the other half?
choices: Pause the campaign and reallocate the rest
Spend it identically so the first half was not wasted
Double the same ads to overwhelm the data
Spend it on office decorations instead
correctAnswer: Pause the campaign and reallocate the rest
correctExplanation: Right. The spent half bought a lesson — wrong channel — and lessons say redirect. Spending the rest identically turns tuition into arson.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to pause the campaign and reallocate the rest. Zero leads from half a budget is data, not bad luck to average out. Every budget needs a stop-loss written before launch.
lessonContent:
Zero results from half a budget is an answer, not a streak.
Stop-losses belong in marketing plans as well as trading ones.
Tuition spending teaches; continuation spending burns.
Reallocate fast — channels rarely fix themselves.
Share this: set a stop-loss number on one spending line.

title: The Doubled Quote
question: Your kitchen is half renovated when the contractor doubles the remaining price. A rival quotes the whole job, from scratch, at the original total. What is rational?
choices: Pay double to protect the half-finished work
Finish it yourself with no skills to save face
Beg the contractor to feel ashamed
Switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen
correctAnswer: Switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen
correctExplanation: Correct. The half-done kitchen exists in all futures; only remaining cost differs. Paying double 'protects' nothing — it ransoms your own project.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to switch contractors despite the half-done kitchen. Progress-to-date is sunk leverage the contractor is exploiting. Get completion quotes, not sympathy, and let the rival finish it.
lessonContent:
Half-done work is sunk leverage — never let it become a ransom.
Always price completion, not continuation.
Mid-project repricing is information about the contractor.
Competitive quotes are the antidote to capture.
Share this: get a completion quote on anything stalled.

title: The Wrong Major
question: Two years into an accounting degree you dread, switching to design adds one extra year but fits you far better. What does clear thinking say?
choices: Stay, because two years must not be wasted
Switch majors and accept the extra year
Stay and be miserable out of loyalty to sunk semesters
Pick whichever annoys your advisor most
correctAnswer: Switch majors and accept the extra year
correctExplanation: Yes. The two years are spent in all futures; the choice is between three content years and two miserable ones. One extra year is cheap against a forty-year career.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to switch majors and accept the extra year. Sunk semesters feel enormous at twenty and tiny at forty. Compare careers, not transcripts — the degree serves the life, not vice versa.
lessonContent:
Degrees serve lives, not transcripts.
Two painful years are a scouting report, not a life sentence.
One extra year is trivial against a forty-year career.
Choose the future self you want to inhabit.
Share this: ask a graduate what they would switch with hindsight.

title: The Weak Hand
question: The poker pot is huge, but your cards are weak and one more bet is required to stay. The chips you already committed cannot be retrieved. What is disciplined?
choices: Stay in, because the pot is huge
Call to defend everything you already committed
Fold and ignore the chips already committed
Borrow money to win it all back
correctAnswer: Fold and ignore the chips already committed
correctExplanation: Correct. Pot size tempts, but your cards decide — and committed chips are gone either way. 'Pot committed' with a dead hand is just donating with drama.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to fold and ignore the chips already committed. Big pots lure weak hands the way deep water lures weak swimmers. Decide on card strength and price, never on chips already pushed forward.
lessonContent:
Chips pushed forward belong to the pot's past, not your future.
Pot size advertises; card strength decides.
'Pot committed' is often just sunk-cost with a poker face.
Fold early, fold often — survival compounds.
Share this: fold one thing today purely on forward odds.

title: The Cold Curb
question: You waited 25 minutes for a late friend who now says 20 more. A warm café next door beats the freezing curb, and they can join you there. What is sensible?
choices: Head to the café and meet them later
Stand freezing so the 25 minutes meant something
Wait exactly 25 more minutes for symmetry
Walk home in protest
correctAnswer: Head to the café and meet them later
correctExplanation: Right. The 25 minutes are spent; only the next 20 are choosable, and warm beats freezing. Suffering to validate waiting validates nothing.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to head to the café and meet them later. Freezing to honor the wait converts sunk minutes into a cold. Redirect the meeting point instead of enduring the curb.
lessonContent:
Waiting validates nothing — comfort is still choosable.
Redirect plans instead of enduring them.
Sunk minutes feel like investments; they are weather.
Propose the warm alternative before resentment arrives.
Share this: move one waiting plan indoors this week.

title: The Tired Engine
question: Your old car worth $800 needs a $900 repair, with the mechanic warning more is coming. What is the clear-eyed call?
choices: Repair it, because you already spent so much on it before
Repair it twice to show the car who is boss
Sell it for parts and start over
Retire the car instead of funding another repair
correctAnswer: Retire the car instead of funding another repair
correctExplanation: Correct. Past repairs are sunk; this $900 buys a fraction of an $800 car plus looming bills. Price the car's future, not its history with you.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to retire the car instead of funding another repair. Every old repair is gone, and warnings of more are forward costs in disguise. Compare repair bills against replacement, never against nostalgia.
lessonContent:
Price the machine's future, not your history together.
Repair-versus-replace is arithmetic wearing overalls.
'Just one more fix' is the car's favorite sentence.
Looming warnings are costs arriving early — heed them.
Share this: total one possession's repair history honestly.

title: The Final Season
question: You endured five bad seasons of a show, and the final season just dropped. Watching costs eight hours; everyone agrees it stays bad. What is smart?
choices: Watch it, or the five seasons were pointless
Watch it at double speed to halve the waste
Skip the finale and reclaim your evenings
Rewatch season one to remember why you started
correctAnswer: Skip the finale and reclaim your evenings
correctExplanation: Yes. The five seasons are unwatched-able history; only eight future hours are at stake. Completionism is sunk-cost with a trophy screen.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to skip the finale and reclaim your evenings. Endured seasons don't obligate future ones — quitting at the finale still banks every hour saved. Spoil yourself with a summary instead.
lessonContent:
Completionism is sunk-cost with a trophy screen.
Summaries exist precisely for shows you should quit.
Hours saved at the finale spend identically to any others.
Abandon franchises, not just books.
Share this: read a plot summary instead of a final season.

title: The Expiring Points
question: Your loyalty points expire soon, tempting you toward a trip you don't want on bad dates. What is the points-smart move?
choices: Take the trip so the points do not die in vain
Let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike
Book the trip and resent every mile of it
Buy overpriced merchandise to rescue the balance
correctAnswer: Let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike
correctExplanation: Correct. Points are sunk discounts, not obligations — spending a miserable week to 'save' them buys the most expensive free trip ever. Expiry is a feature that frees you.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to let the points expire rather than take a trip you dislike. Loyalty programs monetize exactly this dread of waste. A free trip you hate costs a week of your life.
lessonContent:
Loyalty currencies buy loyalty, not value.
Expiry dread is the program working as designed.
Free things that cost weeks are the priciest of all.
Let balances die before they spend your life.
Share this: let one expiring balance go without a flinch.

title: The Split Sauce
question: Your sauce split, and rescuing it needs pricey saffron with poor odds. Restarting from scratch costs little and twenty minutes. What is wise?
choices: Restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively
Pour saffron after pride and hope loudly
Serve it split and blame the recipe
Throw the whole dinner away in despair
correctAnswer: Restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively
correctExplanation: Right. The split batch is sunk; compare rescue cost against restart cost. Cheap restarts beat expensive rescues nearly every time.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to restart the sauce instead of rescuing it expensively. Pride prescribes saffron; arithmetic prescribes twenty minutes. Rescue spending should beat restart spending, or restart wins.
lessonContent:
Compare rescue cost against restart cost, not against zero.
Pride prescribes premium ingredients; arithmetic prescribes fresh starts.
Split sauces and sunk projects share one decision rule.
Restarting is a skill disguised as defeat.
Share this: restart one small thing instead of rescuing it.

title: The Bare Soil
question: Your seedlings never sprouted after a month, but daily watering continues from habit. Fresh seeds plus two weeks beats another month of hope. What now?
choices: Keep watering faithfully until autumn
Water twice as much to encourage the soil
Buy a garden gnome to supervise
Replant the bed instead of watering bare soil
correctAnswer: Replant the bed instead of watering bare soil
correctExplanation: Correct. The month of watering is sunk; bare soil plus hope is not a crop. Replanting converts ritual into results in two weeks.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to replant the bed instead of watering bare soil. Habit waters; evidence replants. A month with zero sprouts is the soil's verdict — appeal it with fresh seeds, not more water.
lessonContent:
Habit waters; evidence replants.
Zero results over a full cycle is a verdict, not a delay.
Rituals feel productive while producing nothing.
Appeal bad verdicts with fresh starts, not more of the same.
Share this: replant one habit-bed you have been watering bare.

title: The Silent Guitar
question: You bought a pricey guitar but dislike practicing; selling it funds piano lessons you would love. What is the music-smart move?
choices: Keep the guitar as expensive wall decoration
Practice miserably to justify the purchase
Sell the guitar and fund piano lessons
Buy a second guitar for motivation
correctAnswer: Sell the guitar and fund piano lessons
correctExplanation: Yes. The purchase price is sunk; the guitar's value now is whatever it funds. Loving piano beats resenting strings at any price.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to sell the guitar and fund piano lessons. Justifying purchases with misery converts one sunk cost into years of dull practice. Instruments serve players, never the reverse.
lessonContent:
Possessions serve players, never the reverse.
Resale converts mistakes into tuition for better ones.
Loving the instrument beats affording it.
Miserable practice justifies nothing — redirect it.
Share this: sell one guilt-possession and fund something loved.

title: The Second Day
question: You paid $500 for a two-day conference; day one was useless and day two promises the same speakers. What buys the most value?
choices: Attend day two so the $500 counts
Sleep through day two in the back row
Skip day two and work on what matters
Heckle the speakers to recover value
correctAnswer: Skip day two and work on what matters
correctExplanation: Correct. The $500 is gone; day two is a fresh eight hours. Spending it proving attendance wastes the only asset left — your time.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is to skip day two and work on what matters. Attendance theater recovers no value. Day one was the sample; its verdict is the gift — accept it and redeploy.
lessonContent:
Day one of anything is a paid sample.
Attendance theater recovers zero value.
Redeploy rescued hours immediately or they dissolve.
Bad conferences teach decisiveness as a side effect.
Share this: skip the second half of one bad event.

title: The Third Rescue
question: Executives funded two rescue rounds for a failing product; both flopped. Now a third rescue is requested with the same plan. What is disciplined?
choices: Cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds
Fund round three because the first two must pay off
Fund it to avoid admitting the rescues failed
Rename the product and fund it quietly
correctAnswer: Cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds
correctExplanation: Exactly. Two failed rescues are evidence, not investment — the same plan failing twice predicts the third. Escalation ends when evidence outranks embarrassment.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is to cancel the project despite the two rescue rounds. Failed rescues are data about the plan, and identical plans don't improve with repetition. This is the Concorde trap: flying on because so much was spent.
lessonContent:
Failed rescues are evidence, not installments toward success.
Identical plans do not improve with repetition.
Escalation ends when evidence outranks embarrassment.
Famous money pits (Concorde!) all flew on sunk fuel.
Share this: name one project surviving on rescue rounds.
